loc_todomvc.title: Lines of code (TodoMVC)
loc_todomvc.human: Fewer lines to read when someone else picks the project up. Counts the code you write and maintain yourself, not a stylesheet you installed from npm.
loc_todomvc.method: Official TodoMVC implementation from github.com/tastejs/todomvc, plus the $mol one from the todomvc-compare repository. Every line of every source file under `src/`, tests, build config and the HTML shell excluded. Styles are excluded for every framework, because TodoMVC renders one fixed layout and its CSS is the same work regardless of framework: the tastejs examples install that stylesheet as the `todomvc-app-css` package and keep a small override sheet, while the $mol implementation writes its own. Counting styles would compare that packaging choice rather than the frameworks. The counting rule is the one published in todomvc-compare and reproduces its $mol figure to the line.

deps_runtime.title: npm packages shipped
deps_runtime.human: How many npm packages end up inside the bundle the browser downloads. This is code your users execute, not code your build machine reads.
deps_runtime.method: Distinct `node_modules/<package>` paths in the `sources` of the production build sourcemaps. Scaffolded on 2026-08-13 with each framework's own getting-started command: react `npm create vite@latest app -- --template react-ts`; vue `npm create vue@latest app -- --default`; svelte `npx sv create app --template minimal --types ts --no-add-ons --install npm`; solid `npm create solid@latest app -- --vanilla --ts --template basic`; angular `npx @angular/cli@21 new app --defaults --skip-git --package-manager=npm`; $mol `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/hyoo-ru/mam.git app && npm install`. For $mol, the sourcemap of the deployed todomvc.hyoo.ru bundle.

deps_direct.title: Dev dependencies declared
deps_direct.human: Packages the starter project names in its own package.json. Build-time tooling included: this is the list your development environment inherits, not what reaches the browser.
deps_direct.method: Entries in `dependencies` plus `devDependencies` of a fresh starter project. Scaffolded on 2026-08-13 with each framework's own getting-started command: react `npm create vite@latest app -- --template react-ts`; vue `npm create vue@latest app -- --default`; svelte `npx sv create app --template minimal --types ts --no-add-ons --install npm`; solid `npm create solid@latest app -- --vanilla --ts --template basic`; angular `npx @angular/cli@21 new app --defaults --skip-git --package-manager=npm`; $mol `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/hyoo-ru/mam.git app && npm install`.

deps_transitive.title: Dev packages installed
deps_transitive.human: How many separate packages npm resolves into node_modules on a clean checkout. Each one is an author your build trusts, and every CI run downloads all of them.
deps_transitive.method: Distinct name+version pairs in `npm ls --all` after scaffolding and installing the starter project. Scaffolded on 2026-08-13 with each framework's own getting-started command: react `npm create vite@latest app -- --template react-ts`; vue `npm create vue@latest app -- --default`; svelte `npx sv create app --template minimal --types ts --no-add-ons --install npm`; solid `npm create solid@latest app -- --vanilla --ts --template basic`; angular `npx @angular/cli@21 new app --defaults --skip-git --package-manager=npm`; $mol `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/hyoo-ru/mam.git app && npm install`.

node_modules_size.title: node_modules size
node_modules_size.human: Disk footprint of a fresh checkout. None of it ships to the browser, but all of it is downloaded by every CI run and every new machine on the team.
node_modules_size.method: `du -sk node_modules` after scaffolding and installing the starter project. Scaffolded on 2026-08-13 with each framework's own getting-started command: react `npm create vite@latest app -- --template react-ts`; vue `npm create vue@latest app -- --default`; svelte `npx sv create app --template minimal --types ts --no-add-ons --install npm`; solid `npm create solid@latest app -- --vanilla --ts --template basic`; angular `npx @angular/cli@21 new app --defaults --skip-git --package-manager=npm`; $mol `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/hyoo-ru/mam.git app && npm install`.

bundle_gzip.title: TodoMVC bundle, gzip
bundle_gzip.human: What the browser actually downloads for a small but complete application, compressed the way a server would send it.
bundle_gzip.method: Every JavaScript and CSS asset referenced by the production `index.html`, gzipped at level 9 and summed. Unlike the line count, styling is included everywhere and is comparable: the shared `todomvc-app-css` is compiled into each tastejs example’s shipped CSS, and $mol compiles its styles into the JavaScript bundle, leaving its `web.css` a 38-byte comment. The `base.js` page furniture from `todomvc-common` is excluded everywhere, including its Angular equivalent. Built artifacts come from the tastejs repository; the $mol bundle from the deployed todomvc.hyoo.ru.

startup_bytes.title: Startup transfer
startup_bytes.human: Bytes pulled over the network before the benchmark application is usable. Same application in every column, so the difference is the framework.
startup_bytes.method: Lighthouse total byte weight for the js-framework-benchmark application, reported as benchmark 34_startup-totalbytes. Transfer size, not gzip specifically.

create_1k.title: Create 1,000 rows
create_1k.human: Time to put a thousand fresh rows on the screen. This is the wait after hitting a filter or opening a list.

update_1k.title: Partial update
update_1k.human: Touching every tenth row of a thousand, sixteen times. This is where a framework either finds the changed rows or re-checks everything.

swap_rows.title: Swap two rows
swap_rows.human: Two rows trade places out of a thousand. The ideal answer is two DOM moves, and the gap here shows who gets close to it.

remove_row.title: Remove one row
remove_row.human: Deleting a single row out of a thousand. The smallest possible change, so it measures the fixed cost of reacting at all.

mem_ready.title: Memory after load
mem_ready.human: Heap the framework occupies with nothing on the page yet.

mem_1k.title: Memory with 1,000 rows
mem_1k.human: Heap once a thousand rows are on screen. On a phone this is the difference between staying alive in the background and being killed.

startup_tbt.title: Startup blocking time
startup_tbt.human: How long the main thread is busy during startup, so taps and scrolls do nothing.
startup_tbt.method: js-framework-benchmark 32_startup-bt (Lighthouse total blocking time), arithmetic mean of 4 runs.

router.title: Router
router.human: Whether URLs and navigation come from the framework project itself, or you go pick a library and own that choice forever.
router.method: Built in means the framework project ships it itself: its own package, or one the same team maintains and publishes as official. A library from anyone else counts as no, however popular or de-facto standard it has become, which is why routing is a yes for Angular and a no for React. The same cut is applied to all six frameworks, and every value links to the official page it was read from. Yes when that project publishes and documents a routing solution of its own. No when its own docs send you to a third-party project instead.

i18n.title: Localization
i18n.human: Translating an application is rarely planned at the start and always arrives later.
i18n.method: Built in means the framework project ships it itself: its own package, or one the same team maintains and publishes as official. A library from anyone else counts as no, however popular or de-facto standard it has become, which is why routing is a yes for Angular and a no for React. The same cut is applied to all six frameworks, and every value links to the official page it was read from. Yes when that project publishes and documents localization of its own. An official CLI add-on that wires up somebody else’s i18n library is a no, because the library is still somebody else’s.

themes.title: Theming
themes.human: Dark mode and brand colours without inventing your own CSS variable convention.
themes.method: Built in means the framework project ships it itself: its own package, or one the same team maintains and publishes as official. A library from anyone else counts as no, however popular or de-facto standard it has become, which is why routing is a yes for Angular and a no for React. The same cut is applied to all six frameworks, and every value links to the official page it was read from. Yes when that project publishes and documents a theming mechanism of its own. No when the word does not appear in its official API reference, which is the page linked, so the absence can be checked directly.

virtual.title: List virtualization
virtual.human: Long lists stay smooth because off-screen rows are never rendered. Without it, someone eventually bolts a library onto a list that already shipped.
virtual.method: Built in means the framework project ships it itself: its own package, or one the same team maintains and publishes as official. A library from anyone else counts as no, however popular or de-facto standard it has become, which is why routing is a yes for Angular and a no for React. The same cut is applied to all six frameworks, and every value links to the official page it was read from. Yes when that project publishes and documents lazy or virtual rendering of long lists. No when no such component appears in its API reference.

offline.title: Offline support
offline.human: A service worker set up by the framework rather than copied from a blog post.
offline.method: Built in means the framework project ships it itself: its own package, or one the same team maintains and publishes as official. A library from anyone else counts as no, however popular or de-facto standard it has become, which is why routing is a yes for Angular and a no for React. The same cut is applied to all six frameworks, and every value links to the official page it was read from. Yes when that project ships the service worker integration: a module it builds and registers for you. No when the docs only show where to drop your own sw.js and how to register it with the browser API, because that is the browser’s feature rather than the framework’s.

ssr.title: Server rendering
ssr.human: Rendering to HTML on the server, for search engines and for the first paint.
ssr.method: Built in means the framework project ships it itself: its own package, or one the same team maintains and publishes as official. A library from anyone else counts as no, however popular or de-facto standard it has become, which is why routing is a yes for Angular and a no for React. The same cut is applied to all six frameworks, and every value links to the official page it was read from. Yes when that project publishes and documents a server rendering API of its own. No when its published module list contains no such module.

tests_nodom.title: Tests without a DOM
tests_nodom.human: Components testable as plain objects, with no browser and no jsdom to boot up first.
tests_nodom.method: Built in means the framework project ships it itself: its own package, or one the same team maintains and publishes as official. A library from anyone else counts as no, however popular or de-facto standard it has become, which is why routing is a yes for Angular and a no for React. The same cut is applied to all six frameworks, and every value links to the official page it was read from. Yes when components can be instantiated and asserted on with no document in play. No when a DOM has to exist before a component renders at all, whether because the official testing guide prescribes jsdom, happy-dom or a browser, or because the framework’s own test runtime boots one.

di.title: Dependency injection
di.human: Swapping a real service for a fake one in a test without touching the component that uses it.
di.method: Built in means the framework project ships it itself: its own package, or one the same team maintains and publishes as official. A library from anyone else counts as no, however popular or de-facto standard it has become, which is why routing is a yes for Angular and a no for React. The same cut is applied to all six frameworks, and every value links to the official page it was read from. Yes when that project documents a way to hand a component a value from outside it and replace that value later, in a test or in another host. Context APIs count: the bar is a documented mechanism, not a particular shape of container.

forms.title: Forms
forms.human: Validation, dirty state and submission handled by the framework instead of a fourth form library per team.
forms.method: Built in means the framework project ships it itself: its own package, or one the same team maintains and publishes as official. A library from anyone else counts as no, however popular or de-facto standard it has become, which is why routing is a yes for Angular and a no for React. The same cut is applied to all six frameworks, and every value links to the official page it was read from. Yes when that project documents a form API that goes past binding one input to one variable, covering at least submission handling or validation state. Two-way binding on its own is a no.

typed_templates.title: Typed templates
typed_templates.human: A typo in a template is caught by the compiler, not by a user.
typed_templates.method: Built in means the framework project ships it itself: its own package, or one the same team maintains and publishes as official. A library from anyone else counts as no, however popular or de-facto standard it has become, which is why routing is a yes for Angular and a no for React. The same cut is applied to all six frameworks, and every value links to the official page it was read from. Yes when the framework’s official TypeScript documentation covers type checking of its template or view layer.

stars.title: GitHub stars
stars.human: A popularity signal, and nothing more. It says how many people bookmarked the repository, not how many shipped with it.
stars.method: `stargazers_count` from the GitHub API for the repository that holds the framework's current source.

npm_downloads.title: npm downloads
npm_downloads.human: The closest thing to a usage count. Inflated by CI runs, but inflated the same way for everyone.
npm_downloads.method: npm registry downloads for the last full week, for the package you install to use the framework.

so_questions.title: Stack Overflow questions
so_questions.human: How likely it is that your problem was already asked and answered by someone else.
so_questions.method: Question count of the framework's Stack Overflow tag, via the Stack Exchange API.

maintainers.title: npm maintainers
maintainers.human: How many people can publish a release. A low number is a bus factor.
maintainers.method: Length of the `maintainers` array in the npm registry metadata of the framework's primary package.

cve_runtime.title: Advisories in shipped packages
cve_runtime.human: Known vulnerabilities in the packages that reach the browser. These execute on your users’ machines, which makes them a different class of risk from anything in the build toolchain.
cve_runtime.method: Each shipped package, at its installed version, queried against the OSV database. Counts packages carrying at least one advisory.

cve_tree.title: Advisories in the dev tree
cve_tree.human: Known vulnerabilities in the packages a fresh checkout installs. These run on developer and CI machines rather than in the browser, but somebody still has to triage every one.
cve_tree.method: Total reported by `npm audit` on the starter project, straight after scaffolding it. Scaffolded on 2026-08-13 with each framework's own getting-started command: react `npm create vite@latest app -- --template react-ts`; vue `npm create vue@latest app -- --default`; svelte `npx sv create app --template minimal --types ts --no-add-ons --install npm`; solid `npm create solid@latest app -- --vanilla --ts --template basic`; angular `npx @angular/cli@21 new app --defaults --skip-git --package-manager=npm`; $mol `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/hyoo-ru/mam.git app && npm install`.

breaking_3y.title: Breaking releases in 3 years
breaking_3y.human: Major versions shipped since 2023. Every one of them is a migration someone on the team pays for.
breaking_3y.method: Count of major semver versions of the framework's primary npm package first published in the last three years. Left blank for packages that do not use semver majors.
